summary.text: Let \(B_0=4,B_1=16,B_2=63\) and \(B_{n+3}=4B_{n+2}-B_n\), and define the defect \(D_n=B_{n+1}^2-B_nB_{n+2}\); its recurrence \(D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n\), together with growth bounds for \(B_n\), inductively gives \(0<D_n\le B_n\). Thus \(B_{n+1}^2=B_nB_{n+2}+D_n\) forces \(\lceil B_{n+1}^2/B_n\rceil-1=B_{n+2}\), so the original nonlinear sequence equals \(B\) and hence satisfies the linear recurrence corresponding to the claimed generating function.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) denote the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
a_0=4,\qquad a_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\), \(a_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer for which
\[
\frac{a_{n+2}}{a_{n+1}}<\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}.
\]
Once positivity of the terms is known, this condition is equivalent to
\[
a_{n+2}<\frac{a_{n+1}^2}{a_n}.
\]
For any real number \(r\), the greatest integer strictly less than \(r\) is \(\lceil r\rceil-1\), including when \(r\) itself is an integer. Hence the original rule can be written as
\[
a_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{a_{n+1}^2}{a_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{1}
\]
We will construct a positive integer sequence satisfying (1), prove that it is the sequence \((a_n)\), and then read off its linear recurrence and generating function.

Define an auxiliary sequence \((B_n)_{n\ge0}\), initially as a sequence of integers, by
\[
B_0=4,\qquad B_1=16,\qquad B_2=63,
\]
and
\[
B_{n+3}=4B_{n+2}-B_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{2}
\]
Its first few terms are
\[
4,16,63,248,976,3841,\ldots,
\]
as expected. We must show that the nonlinear ceiling rule (1) produces exactly this linear-recurrence sequence.

First we establish positivity and sufficient growth of \(B_n\). We claim that for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
B_n>0\qquad\text{and}\qquad 3B_n\le B_{n+1}. \tag{3}
\]
For \(n=0,1,2\), this follows directly from
\[
B_0=4,\quad B_1=16,\quad B_2=63,\quad B_3=4\cdot63-4=248:
\]
indeed \(12\le16\), \(48\le63\), and \(189\le248\).

Suppose now that (3) is known at the indices \(n,n+1,n+2\). In particular,
\[
B_{n+1}\ge3B_n,
\qquad
B_{n+2}\ge3B_{n+1}\ge9B_n.
\]
Consequently
\[
B_{n+3}=4B_{n+2}-B_n>0.
\]
For the growth estimate at the next index, use (2) twice:
\[
B_{n+4}=4B_{n+3}-B_{n+1}.
\]
Thus \(B_{n+4}\ge3B_{n+3}\) is equivalent to \(B_{n+3}\ge B_{n+1}\). But
\[
B_{n+3}-B_{n+1}=4B_{n+2}-B_n-B_{n+1}>0,
\]
for example because \(B_{n+2}\ge3B_{n+1}\) and \(B_{n+1}\ge3B_n>0\). This proves (3) for all \(n\) by induction. In particular, all the \(B_n\) are positive integers, so from now on they may be regarded as natural numbers as well.

The key quantity is the defect
\[
D_n:=B_{n+1}^2-B_nB_{n+2}. \tag{4}
\]
It measures how far \(B_{n+1}^2/B_n\) lies above the integer \(B_{n+2}\). We will prove the sharp-enough bounds
\[
1\le D_n\le B_n \qquad(n\ge0). \tag{5}
\]

The defects themselves satisfy a simple recurrence. Substituting (2) into (4) and expanding gives
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n. \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, this is obtained by writing
\[
B_{n+3}=4B_{n+2}-B_n,
\quad
B_{n+4}=4B_{n+3}-B_{n+1},
\quad
B_{n+5}=4B_{n+4}-B_{n+2}
\]
in
\(D_{n+3}=B_{n+4}^2-B_{n+3}B_{n+5}\); after cancellation, the result is
\[
4\bigl(B_{n+2}^2-B_{n+1}B_{n+3}\bigr)
 +\bigl(B_{n+1}^2-B_nB_{n+2}\bigr)
=4D_{n+1}+D_n.
\]
The initial defects are
\[
D_0=16^2-4\cdot63=4,
\]
\[
D_1=63^2-16\cdot248=1,
\]
and
\[
D_2=248^2-63\cdot976=16. \tag{7}
\]
They are all positive. Equation (6) then proves inductively that every \(D_n\) is positive: when proving positivity of \(D_{n+3}\), both \(D_{n+1}\) and \(D_n\) are positive and
\(D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n\). Since the defects are integers, positivity gives \(D_n\ge1\), which is the lower bound in (5).

We next prove the upper bound \(D_n\le B_n\). It holds at the first three indices by (7):
\[
D_0=4=B_0,
\qquad D_1=1\le16=B_1,
\qquad D_2=16\le63=B_2.
\]
Suppose inductively that
\[
D_n\le B_n\qquad\text{and}\qquad D_{n+1}\le B_{n+1}.
\]
Then (6) gives
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n\le4B_{n+1}+B_n. \tag{8}
\]
On the other hand, by (2),
\[
B_{n+3}=4B_{n+2}-B_n.
\]
The growth estimates (3) imply
\[
4B_{n+1}+B_n\le4B_{n+2}-B_n. \tag{9}
\]
For completeness, subtracting the left side of (9) from the right side gives
\[
4(B_{n+2}-B_{n+1})-2B_n.
\]
Since \(B_{n+2}\ge3B_{n+1}\), this is at least
\(8B_{n+1}-2B_n\), which is positive because \(B_{n+1}\ge3B_n>0\). Combining (8) and (9) yields
\[
D_{n+3}\le B_{n+3}.
\]
Together with the three initial cases, this proves the upper bound for every index. We have therefore established (5).

We now apply these defect bounds to the ceiling recurrence. From the definition of \(D_n\),
\[
B_{n+1}^2=B_nB_{n+2}+D_n. \tag{10}
\]
Because \(B_n>0\) and \(1\le D_n\le B_n\), division by \(B_n\) gives
\[
B_{n+2}<\frac{B_{n+1}^2}{B_n}\le B_{n+2}+1. \tag{11}
\]
It follows immediately that
\[
\left\lceil\frac{B_{n+1}^2}{B_n}\right\rceil=B_{n+2}+1,
\]
and hence
\[
B_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{B_{n+1}^2}{B_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{12}
\]
Thus \((B_n)\) satisfies precisely the original nonlinear recurrence.

Equivalently, in integer-division form, the elementary fact being used is the following. If natural numbers \(x,y,z,d\) satisfy
\[
x=yz+d,\qquad 1\le d\le y,
\]
then
\[
z<\frac{x}{y}\le z+1,
\]
so
\[
\left\lceil\frac{x}{y}\right\rceil-1=z.
\]
Since for positive \(y\),
\[
\left\lceil\frac{x}{y}\right\rceil=\frac{x+y-1}{y}
\]
with the division on the right being integer quotient, this also says
\[
\frac{x+y-1}{y}-1=z.
\]
Applying this with
\[
x=B_{n+1}^2,
\quad y=B_n,
\quad z=B_{n+2},
\quad d=D_n
\]
is exactly (12).

It remains to identify \(B_n\) with the sequence from the original definition. This follows by strong induction. At indices \(0\) and \(1\), both sequences have the prescribed values \(4\) and \(16\). Suppose \(n=k+2\ge2\) and that equality has already been proved at all smaller indices, in particular at \(k\) and \(k+1\). Then the original recurrence (1), the induction hypothesis, and (12) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{k+2}
&=\left\lceil\frac{a_{k+1}^2}{a_k}\right\rceil-1\\
&=\left\lceil\frac{B_{k+1}^2}{B_k}\right\rceil-1\\
&=B_{k+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
a_n=B_n\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0. \tag{13}
\]
This argument also proves positivity of every term in the originally defined sequence, justifying all ratio and ceiling manipulations above.

Transferring the defining linear recurrence (2) through (13), we obtain
\[
a_0=4,
\qquad a_1=16,
\qquad a_2=63,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge3\),
\[
a_n=4a_{n-1}-a_{n-3}. \tag{14}
\]
There is no ambiguity from subtraction in the natural numbers: the right side is nonnegative because it equals the positive integer \(B_n\); alternatively, (3) immediately gives more than enough growth to ensure \(B_{n-3}\le4B_{n-1}\).

Finally, let
\[
G(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary generating function, interpreted as a formal power series. Multiply by \(1-4x+x^3\). Its constant coefficient is
\[
a_0=4.
\]
Its coefficient of \(x\) is
\[
a_1-4a_0=16-16=0,
\]
and its coefficient of \(x^2\) is
\[
a_2-4a_1=63-64=-1.
\]
For every \(n\ge3\), the coefficient of \(x^n\) is
\[
a_n-4a_{n-1}+a_{n-3},
\]
which is zero by (14). Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)=4-x^2.
\]
Since the denominator has constant term \(1\), it is invertible as a formal power series, and hence
\[
\boxed{G(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
This proves the conjectured generating function for the sequence produced by the original, non-alternating extremal consecutive-ratio definition.
